canberra.title: ASD report highlights increasing number of AI-enabled cyber threats
canberra.snippet: The Federal Government has released the Australian Signals Directorate’s (ASD) Annual Cyber Threat Report for 2025-26, and it shows an in...
canberra.content:
The Australian Signals Directorate’s Annual Cyber Threat Report shows the increasing use of AI in cyber threats. Photo: ASD.

The Federal Government has released the Australian Signals Directorate’s (ASD) Annual Cyber Threat Report for 2025-26, and it shows an increase in malicious cyber activity and incidents.

Produced by ASD’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC), the report recognises that artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been a key factor in the cyber threat landscape in the year to 30 June. It says the use of AI, more than ever before, has allowed malicious actors to identify and exploit vulnerabilities at a greater scale, speed and sophistication to conduct espionage, steal money and disrupt systems.

“Technology is evolving at accelerated rates and continues to impact cyber security in both positive and negative ways,” the ACSC says.

“Throughout FY2025-26, AI tools became more accessible, driven by a new generation of frontier AI models. These models have changed the game with speed and opportunity, but they have also generated significant uncertainty.

“The question is no longer whether organisations will face cyber threats, but how prepared they are to respond.”

The ACSC says the likelihood of cyber incidents has increased by more than 20 per cent over the previous year, and Australian organisations need to take action accordingly.

The ACSC also found that incidents of potential malicious cyber activity rose to more than 4400, almost 80 per cent more than last year, and the ASD responded to more than 1500 cyber security incidents, 300 more than last year and a spike of 36 per cent over the past five years.

While raising awareness of the increased use of AI in cyber incidents, ASD also said it could be useful in defending against such attacks.

“To respond effectively to these new threats, organisations must strengthen patching processes and adapt basic cyber security controls to remain resilient,” the report reads.

“Equally, the integration of AI tools into organisations’ security operations can facilitate the early detection of vulnerabilities, enhance software quality, monitor for unusual behaviour and improve incident response times.”

In the reporting period, the ACSC received more than 82,000 cybercrime reports, an average of one every six minutes, and answered more than 37,500 calls to the Australian Cyber Security Hotline, or 102 notifications a day.

In response, it published 76 alerts, advisories and publications on its cyber.gov.au website, including a range of joint products with international partners.

ASD’s Australian Cyber Security Centre received 82,000 cybercrime reports in 2025-26. Photo: ASD.

The report showed the growing impact of cybercrime on Australians and Australian organisations, with ASD’s Australian Protective Domain Name System processing more than 220 billion queries and blocking access to more than 564 million malicious domains last year.

It says the average self-reported cost of cybercrime remained at $33,000 for individuals, but rose more than 16 per cent to $93,500 for businesses.

The ACSC also says state-sponsored cyber actors have again targeted Australian organisations, primarily to gain access to sensitive or non-public information.

It says this activity extends beyond government networks, and includes critical infrastructure entities, private businesses and individuals.

“As the global security environment continues to deteriorate, state-sponsored cyber actors are increasingly seeking to pre-position within networks to enable future intelligence collection, disruption or access to higher-value targets at a time of their choosing,” it says.

“This trend is not confined to Australia and is evident in the context of multiple global conflicts currently underway. Cyber is normalised as a feature of conventional warfare.”

Minister for Defence Richard Marles said the Annual Cyber Threat Report reflected the fact that Australia continued to face a challenging strategic environment, with AI accelerating the scale, speed and complexity of cyber threats.

“AI is reshaping the online landscape, enabling cybercriminals and state-sponsored actors to launch faster, more sophisticated and scalable attacks,” Mr Marles said.

To stay ahead, Australians must enhance their cyber defences while harnessing AI’s benefits.

“The Annual Cyber Threat Report reinforces that government and industry must continue to work together to strengthen our collective cyber resilience and safeguard our critical digital infrastructure.”

Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Cyber Security Tony Burke said cyber security had never been more important, and being under attack was certain, constant and ever-present.

“To keep people safe, we’re positioning Australia to respond to the evolving threats and opportunities presented by emerging technologies,’ Mr Burke said.

“That starts with protecting critical infrastructure and government systems, securing technology at its source and enabling people as our strongest defence to become Australia’s ‘human firewall’.”

In response to the report, the director of the Democracy Counts alliance Tom Mooney said although agencies were doing their job well in handling threats, the onus needed to be placed on tech companies to do the right thing in the first place.

“Artificial intelligence is not ungovernable,” Mr Mooney said. “Australia has a sovereign right to decide how these technologies are used here, and citizens have a democratic right for our leaders to shape the AI transition in a way that puts the public interest before all else.

“Our agencies report that they are working constructively with the companies developing frontier AI, and this presents a real opportunity for Australia to lead.

“The Australian Government needs to ensure companies that develop and deploy AI are accountable to Australians and subject to the law, and we have the opportunity to build a coalition of like-minded countries and tech companies to support establishment of such a regime.”

Original Article published by Andrew McLaughlin on PS News.

canberra.title: Teacher’s aide accused of sexually abusing 15-year-old girl
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse. A teacher’s aide at a Canberra school who also worked as a volleyball ...
canberra.content:
Ezekiel Jeth Cureg, 26, leaves court after pleading not guilty to his charges. Photo: Albert McKnight.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse.

A teacher’s aide at a Canberra school who also worked as a volleyball coach will not be allowed to return to either job after he was accused of sexually abusing an underage girl.

It is alleged 26-year-old Ezekiel Jeth Cureg met the 15-year-old girl through a shared interest in sport before he groomed and sexually assaulted her between September and October 2026.

Mr Cureg had been a volleyball coach and worked as a teacher’s aide in PE at Brindabella Christian College, the ACT Magistrates Court heard. The girl is not a student at the college.

The court heard it was alleged that when he learned the girl had gone to police, he sent her a message that stated something like: “What have you done? What have you said?”.

He was also alleged to have tried to call her about 15 times and contacted one of her friends to ask them about her whereabouts.

He was arrested after police raided his home in Casey and faced the Magistrates Court on Tuesday (27 October) and applied for bail.

The prosecutor, when opposing bail, said the girl was young and vulnerable and it was alleged the man formed an inappropriate relationship with her that “she did not want”.

He was also alleged to have exhibited a significant level of control over her.

“This is an incredibly serious matter,” the prosecutor said.

Ezekiel Jeth Cureg (right) leaves court with his lawyer, Carley Hitchins, after being granted bail. Photo: Albert McKnight.

Carley Hitchins of CODA Criminal Law said her client did not take the allegations lightly, as he had just spent a night in custody for the first time in his life.

She argued he could be released on strict bail conditions, which would go a significant way in reducing the alleged risks of his release.

Magistrate Alexandra Burt said the allegations in the matter described “a significant abuse of power”.

“She is a young person and she is vulnerable,” she said of the girl.

“I accept that on the statement of facts, there has been a flagrant disregard for the complainant and her welfare.”

But she noted Mr Cureg had no criminal history and could reside in the community on very strict bail conditions that were essentially house arrest.

The magistrate granted bail on conditions including he not contact the girl, only leave his home in the company of his parents, not possess a mobile phone or use social media and not be alone around anyone under 18 except for his siblings.

Mr Cureg has entered not guilty pleas to nine counts of committing an act of indecency against a young person, four counts of sexual intercourse with a young person and one count of grooming.

He was seen crying loudly while being comforted by members of his family after he was granted bail.

The matter returns to court on 12 January 2027.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call triple zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

canberra.title: Four-year-old’s parents speak of ‘deep pain’ as his elderly killer faces court
canberra.snippet: The parents of a four-year-old boy killed by an elderly driver when she crashed into him on a Canberra footpath have told a court they li...
canberra.content:
Maureen Brew (insert) admitted killing four-year-old Osal Mayur Pokhrel. Photos: Albert McKnight, supplied.

The parents of a four-year-old boy killed by an elderly driver when she crashed into him on a Canberra footpath have told a court they live with a “very deep pain inside” that is difficult to describe.

But Prakash and Chura Pokhrel finished their moving statement about their son, Osal Mayur Pokhrel, by asking for the “lightest possible sentence” for his killer, so she was able to spend the rest of her life with her own children and grandchildren.

Region has obtained documents that describe how police believe 80-year-old Maureen Brew pressed the accelerator instead of the brake when she drove her car down a footpath at Southlands Shopping Centre in Mawson on 18 January 2026 and crashed into Osal before they ended up inside a liquor store.

His parents and at least 25 bystanders tried to remove items inside the store to reach him, the ACT Supreme Court heard, before four people crawled over broken glass to pull him from under the car.

Tragically, he died shortly afterwards.

During Brew’s sentencing hearing on Tuesday (27 October), the court heard Osal was born in Bhutan before his family moved to Australia and ended up living in Queanbeyan, NSW.

In a statement to the court, his parents described him as “the centre of our lives”.

“Osal was an incredibly loving child. He never hurt anyone and he cherished his family deeply,” they said.

“He always wanted us to do things together and he never missed a chance to show affection.

“His happiness filled our home.”

His parents took him for weekly groceries and then to the park, to see a relative, or they sat down and painted together. They regularly went to the pool, the circus or a magic performance. The family watched movies, went for walks or visited Riverside Plaza in Queanbeyan.

Osal loved his toy cars, ice cream, the film The Lion King, as well as singing in the car. He dreamed of becoming a police officer when he grew up, so he could serve his community

While sharing many memories of him, his parents also told Justice Belinda Baker “there is no way to put his whole life on paper”.

“Four years was not enough for us and it should never have been all he was given,” they said.

“He was loved, he mattered and he is missed every day.”

They also spoke about the grief they continue to feel, saying as time passes they have been finding it harder, not easier, to cope and return to their normal life.

“The life we are leading now will never be same for us even though we have other reasons to live, because losing a child is beyond someone’s imagination,” they said.

“Even after decades and decades, it will be the same pain where we will always miss holding him and not being able see him growing into a big boy.

“We are always grateful to the community for standing with us and sharing our pain.”

Maureen Brew’s car crashed into the Mawson shops on 18 January 2026. Photo: Reddit.

In a statement read to the courtroom, Brew said the crash had a significant impact on her and described it as “a split-second accident”.

“I could not stop thinking of the family, who have suffered so much more,” she said.

Prosecutor Amanda Mifsud disagreed with the defence lawyers’ submission that the crash was caused by Brew’s momentary inattention. She said the facts described “a series of negligent decisions”.

“It is very apparent once you watch the [CCTV] footage,” she said.

“The offender has clearly floored the accelerator in a panicked state.”

Barrister Stephen Dayeian said his client had made a misjudgement when she failed to secure her car and then thought it was secure.

He asked for the court to impose a fully-suspended sentence due to his client’s age and health conditions. He argued the seriousness of her offence fell towards the lower end of the spectrum.

But Ms Mifsud argued a fully-suspended sentence would not reflect the seriousness of the crime.

Brew, who is now 81 and remains living in NSW, pleaded guilty to a charge of culpable driving causing death.

Justice Baker said she would reserve her decision and sentence her at a future date.

“I again thank the parents for an incredibly powerful and gracious victim impact statement which I will be carefully reading many times in the preparation of my sentence reasons in this matter,” she said.

canberra.title: Junee Hotel on the market after Reynoldses put heart and soul into historic pub
canberra.snippet: After breathing new life into one of the Riverina’s most historic pubs, Brendon and Emma Reynolds are ready for their next chapter, and s...
canberra.content:
Brendon and Emma Reynolds are selling the Junee Hotel after transforming the venue. Photo: File.

After breathing new life into one of the Riverina’s most historic pubs, Brendon and Emma Reynolds are ready for their next chapter, and say government red tape is making life increasingly difficult for regional hoteliers.

The couple, who transformed the rundown Junee Hotel into a lively community hub, has put the landmark pub on the market as they look to move closer to family.

But they are determined to leave the hotel in a better state than they found it, with the business operating as usual while they wait for a buyer.

“Life is too short to be away from family so long,” Emma said.

“We’ve worked so hard this past three years and I want a simpler life.”

The couple, originally from Dubbo, took over the lease in May 2023 before buying the property a year later, committing their own money to a building they believed deserved another chance.

What they inherited was a pub in serious disrepair, with filthy accommodation rooms, damaged bathrooms, missing doors and holes in walls.

Since then, they have repainted, replaced carpets, refurbished bathrooms and progressively restored the accommodation while working to bring the bar, bistro and beer garden back to life.

The hotel has 25 rooms available for $90 a night, offering affordable accommodation for travellers and workers, as well as a place for locals to meet.

But the Reynoldses’ biggest contribution may be less about paint and plumbing than the atmosphere they have worked to create.

“We want the place to be somewhere that people can establish a connection,” Emma said.

“People just come into the bar to have a chat. We don’t even expect them to buy anything. People want to be acknowledged; they don’t want a buzzer.”

That philosophy has seen the couple introduce creative events, including a Traffic Light Singles Nght that attracted people from across Australia.

Love match: Alex (left) and Craig (right), with Michael, found quality connections at Junee Hotel’s successful Traffic Light Singles Party. Photo: Marguerite McKinnon.

The concept, designed to help singles meet face-to-face, has reportedly resulted in five relationships, with Emma joking that the next goal was to produce a baby.

“We need to increase Australia’s population,” she said.

The event was such a success it helped inspire a similar singles night at the Punt Hotel in Darlington Point.

The couple has also worked to keep the pub affordable, offering members a permanent happy hour, with selected beers and wines for $6.50.

Emma said the hotel was operating in the black and was being offered at a realistic price, but the challenges facing regional pubs were becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

“The Australian Government are taxing regional pubs like nothing else. Dan Murphy’s don’t get taxed anywhere near as much,” she said.

“Where would you prefer people drinking? At home alone or with people? It’s like a tax on human interaction.”

Staffing was another major headache, with the couple unable to access backpackers seeking regional work to qualify for their second-year visa because of Junee’s postcode.

“The government make things so hard. There’s so much red tape, and staffing is a real challenge,” Emma said.

Her frustration comes amid the couple’s efforts to build a business around personal service, community connection and a historic building that has stood at the centre of Junee for nearly 150 years.

The pub was established as the Railway Hotel in 1878 by Christopher Crawley, before Junee had its own bank, post office or bakery. It served railway workers and travellers, and even functioned as an early railway ticket office.

The Junee Hotel fulfilled its owners’ aim to bring back the ”art of conversation”. Photo: Supplied.

The current building was constructed in 1911-12, with its ornate verandahs, decorative ironwork and high ceilings reflecting the architectural style of the era.

An important part of its history is Elizabeth O’Donnell, an early female licensee who was running the Railway Hotel in the early 1900s, at a time when women were still rare in the licensed trade.

For Emma, the hotel’s significance extends well beyond its commercial value.

“It’s the heart and soul of the Riverina and such an important part of our history. It’s structurally so well done and a beautiful building,” she said.

“We always aim to leave the pub in a much better state than we found it.”

The Reynoldses plan to sell their home and move into the hotel while a sale progresses, noting that regional pubs can take six to 12 months to sell.

In the meantime, the doors remain open, with the couple hoping the next owner will recognise both the potential of the business and the importance of preserving one of Junee’s most recognisable landmarks.

More information on the pub’s sale can be found on the Real Commercial website.

Original Article published by Oliver Jacques on Region Riverina.

canberra.title: Race unicorns, not horses: Compassionate Stakes offers race-day frivolity without welfare worries
canberra.snippet: Canberra’s most unusual race event will return to mark this Melbourne Cup – and there won’t be a horse in sight. Instea...
canberra.content:
“What has surprised me most is how many people felt uneasy about the Cup but had never said so out loud,” said event organiser and local animal welfare advocate Kate Luke. Photo: Supplied.

Canberra’s most unusual race event will return to mark this Melbourne Cup – and there won’t be a horse in sight.

Instead, inflatable unicorns and dinosaurs will thunder through Glebe Park as part of the Compassionate Stakes Festival of Kind Living – a free, family-friendly alternative to the race that stops the nation.

First held in 2019, the Compassionate Stakes aims to provide a fun alternative for those wanting to say ‘nup to the cup’ on race day. This year the event will be held on the Sunday prior to the cup, taking on a new shape and expanding into the inaugural Compassionate Stakes Festival for Kind Living.

“What began as a way of showing there are better ways to have fun than at the expense of animals now looks at the bigger picture,” said organiser Kate Luke.

“The races are still the heart of it, but now we’re looking at the bigger picture too: how the everyday choices we make about the food we eat, the fibre we wear and how we have fun can be kinder to animals and leave a lighter footprint on the planet.”

Award-winning animal welfare advocate Kate Luke, together with her partner James, runs Little Oak Sanctuary.

At their 273-acre off-grid property near Braidwood, the couple and a team of dedicated volunteers currently care for 335 rescued farmed animals, relying entirely on community fundraising to keep their gates open and troughs full.

Kate was recently awarded the Animals Australia Award for Effective Advocacy at the Animal Justice Foundation Awards for her work speaking up for animals, including events like the Compassionate Stakes.

“I won’t lie, it’s been a huge undertaking that does take up our whole lives,” said Kate.

“What keeps me going is watching an animal who arrived terrified learn that people can be safe.”

One such success story is Sunny the sheep, who recently arrived at the sanctuary on death’s door through sheer neglect.

“Just this morning I got to watch him playing – or spronking, which is joy-filled bouncing – with this year’s orphaned lambs and his special-needs sheep friends … that is magic to witness.”

Another long-term resident, Lucky Lago, is a living, breathing example of why Kate encourages scrutiny of the racing industry – and what led her to create the Compassionate Stakes.

Though bred into the racing industry, Lucky was deemed unsuitable at two-years-old and never set foot on the race track.

“The industry has a word for horses like Lucky. It calls them wastage,” said Kate.

“He was on his way to slaughter when he came to us. That’s the part of the industry most people never see.”

Little Oak volunteers Lune and Charline with Sunny the (photogenic) sheep. Photo: Supplied.

Bred for the track but later deemed unsuitable, Lucky Lago was destined for the knackery before he found a home at Little Oak Sanctuary. Photo: Supplied.

Multiple races are held across the day, with the grand final at 2:30 pm. Photo: Supplied.

This year Little Oak Sanctuary will commemorate its 13th anniversary with an Enchanted Garden Gala at The Marion.

“What living with animals teaches you, over and over, is that each one is an individual.

“Cows have best friends. Sheep can recognise faces for years, and remember who was kind or cruel to them. Pigs are smarter than most dogs.

“Once you know them as individuals, it’s very hard to keep a wall up between the animals we call pets and the animals we call products.”

Kate says the Compassionate Stakes simply aims to offer an opportunity to learn about animal welfare in a fun and light-hearted environment.

“On the day, we’re not asking anyone to change their whole life in an afternoon,” she said.

“People come along because they’ve heard the races are hilarious, and plenty of them have no particular view on horse racing when they arrive.

“They spend the day laughing, eating good food, meeting lovely community groups, and somewhere in there the conversation about horses happens naturally.”

Hosted by Canberra’s own Faux Née Phish, multiple heats take place across the day before the Grand Final at 2:30 pm.

Costumes are available for hire, but bookings are essential.

Vegan food offerings include Vietnamese street food from Dickson’s Au Lac restaurant, Majestic Mushrooms from Murrumbateman and Mellabella Gelato from Bungendore.

Plant-inspired workshops and demonstrations will cover culinary crafts like cheese-making and sushi-rolling, while Terrariums Canberra will teach the art of planting mini-gardens in upcycled items.

From dino dance-offs and Jurassic Jenga to clothing swaps and crafternoon tea, Kate says race day frivolity is possible without compromising animal welfare.

“The fun was never in the horses, it was in the people, the costumes, the cheering and the sense of coming together.”

The Compassionate Stakes Festival of Kind Living will take place Sunday 1 November from 10am to 3pm at Glebe Park. Click here for information or costume bookings.

australia.title: ‘Are you waiting for me to be attacked?’ Fatima Payman slams PM over staffing
australia.snippet: Albanese promises ‘swift response’ on MP safety as he mulls panic buttons for politicians Follow our Australian politics live blog for la...
australia.content:
Anthony Albanese has promised a “swift government response” to safety threats to MPs and floated the provision of duress alarms for electorate offices, saying politicians and their staff have put up with threats for too long.

The prime minister’s pledge to the Labor party room came hours after Senator Fatima Payman again slammed her former government colleagues over the lack of staffing given to her office, controversially asking: “Is the prime minister waiting for something, like what happened to Dr Helen Haines, to occur to my office?”

MPs across the political divide have spoken forcefully of the need for more protection for their offices after the alleged attack on the Indi MP last week, raising alarm about threats and violence directed to their staff. Politicians are also revealing the scale of abuse, online and offline, directed toward them, including death and rape threats, with Australia’s eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, telling Senate estimates she and her family had also been subject to online abuse and threats.

In the first Labor party-room meeting since the alleged attack, Albanese gave a long address, saying this week “must be a turning point” for civil discourse and how threats are responded to. He also conceded there needed to be more investment in security and safety for politicians.

Albanese said MPs have had to “put up with the threat environment for too long”, that the government “need to do more” and “more can and should be done”.

“You’ve all dedicated so much to the safety of others in the workplace. I’m determined to make sure we do everything for your safety and the safety of your staff as well,” he said.

Albanese did not give specifics, but promised a “swift government response” on safety, and noted numerous MPs had raised the prospect of receiving duress alarms, or panic buttons, to alert authorities to a safety incident. This was among a “series of options” under consideration.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, also told the meeting that the government was looking at safety at polling booths around election time.

Government sources said numerous changes were being considered, with a full response and proposal likely to be revealed in coming days. MPs have raised a wide range of concerns, including greater security and hardening of their electoral offices, better communication with federal police, and resources for security at their private homes such as CCTV and lighting – all options understood to be under consideration.

An ongoing review into commonwealth workplaces will also be expedited by Labor, with recommendations specifically about safety and security to be delivered soon.

The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, told his MPs in a Coalition party-room meeting of ongoing conversations with the government about personal safety and the importance of getting it right, but did not raise any specific proposals.

Payman speaks out

Payman, who quit Labor in 2024 to sit on the crossbench, on Monday night lashed out at the prime minister for not responding to a request for additional staff in line with other independent political offices.

The prime minister has discretion over the allocation of personal staff, which are typically more senior advisers. All politicians receive electoral office staff, but Payman has zero advisers while 16 other crossbench MPs and senators shared 30 advisers, according to an internal document tabled in the hearing.

In a Senate estimates hearing, Payman questioned the minister Don Farrell whether the staff allocation shortfall was due to Albanese having a personal gripe with her, claiming her staff were severely overworked.

“If [Albanese] cares so much about the welfare and wellbeing of people who work in this building, then I implore you [Farrell] and the prime minister to please look into the fact that my staff are burning out,” she said.

“Is the prime minister waiting for something, like what happened to Dr Helen Haines, to occur to my office – to me – for him to take our request seriously?”

Farrell and other Labor senators in the hearing strongly rejected the insinuation, but Payman refused to withdraw the comments when asked until her staffing request was dealt with.

Payman told Guardian Australia last week there had been a massive increase in the number of death threats and hate comments since 2024 when she defected from Labor. Payman said her office manager had opened mail last year containing human faeces, resulting in a biohazard team having to respond.

“We had all these people in hazmat suits come through [the office],” she said. “The trauma that that inflicts on my staff members is horrible. No office or no worker should ever have to deal with that kind of crap.”

The eSafety commissioner targeted

Inman Grant said in her final appearance before Senate estimates on Tuesday evening that it was a “sensitive and pivotal moment” for parliament in the wake of the alleged attack, and the environment was “dangerously febrile for women in senior government roles”.

“When public officials are used for political point scoring, a target goes on our backs and we are subjected to an onslaught of online abuse and threats,” she said.

“As many of you know, this has been the normal state of affairs for me and my family for years, yet somehow this is meant to be accepted as part of public service.”

Inman Grant did not name any people who have targeted her personally, but her work in the role has seen her labelled as a “censorship commissar” by the world’s richest person, Elon Musk. The US Republican congressman Jim Jordan labelled Inman Grant as a “zealot for global takedowns”.

Inman Grant said more needs to be done for the next generation of leaders to feel safe in online spaces or public-facing roles.

“Social media is no longer the once envisioned digital town square – it has become more like a gladiatorial arena,” she said. “Meanwhile, platforms continue to roll back abuse and violent speech policies that let some of the most egregious offenders out of digital jail.”

australia.title: ABC to demand rightwing One Nation party stop using Bluey in ‘shocking and disrespectful’ cartoon
australia.snippet: Head of Australia’s national broadcaster says depiction of globally beloved character ramming politicians with a car breaches intellectua...
australia.content:
Australia’s national broadcaster will send a cease and desist letter to the rightwing populist party One Nation for using Bluey in a “shocking and disrespectful” cartoon which sees the beloved character repeatedly ramming politicians with an SUV.

The ABC’s managing director, Hugh Marks, told Senate estimates on Tuesday he became aware of One Nation’s potential breach of intellectual property last week and sought legal advice. “We will be taking further action, I can assure you,” he said.

The legal dispute came to light after the Western Australian Labor senator Varun Ghosh asked the ABC if it had sought legal advice over the 2024 political cartoon, called State of Melbourne, which has had 1.3m views on YouTube so far.

“I appreciate it was published two years ago, but has a particular poignancy in the last week,” Ghosh, the communications committee chair, said.

Estimates was held a week after the alleged attack on independent MP Helen Haines outside the politician’s northern Victorian electorate office, which led to her losing both legs.

Marks said he believed the use is a clear breach of intellectual property and “a cease and desist letter should be issued”.

He revealed the ABC had been in contact with Bluey’s international distributor, BBC Studios, and the Brisbane-based creators Ludo. He said Pauline Hanson’s party had not sought permission to use the children’s character in the hit show. The BBC, Ludo and One Nation have been approached for comment.

“It’s not a parody of any Bluey work,” Marks said. “It’s not a minor use of the [intellectual property]. In my view, it is an infringement of the intellectual property, number one. But it’s also a shocking use of Australia’s most loved character.”

“In fact, probably the globally most loved character in a video. That is both shocking and disrespectful to the children of Australia who love that character so much.”

The animation shows Bluey behind the wheel striking a depiction of the former Victorian premier Daniel Andrews and the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, with an SUV, as well as TV host and conservationist Robert Irwin. Before he is run over, the Albanese character says to Bluey: “You’ve got that crazy look in your eyes”.

In one scene in the three-minute video, Andrews is at the wheel, Albanese is his passenger and the car deliberately runs over Bluey and Irwin. The politicians are then shown putting the bodies of Bluey and Irwin in the boot of the SUV.

In the hearing of the environment and communications committee, senators also heard evidence on other matters concerning the ABC.

Marks told them the ABC’s former news director Justin Stevens received a termination payout of $353,230 because he did not want him to work out his notice.

“Following Mr Stevens’s resignation, we had the option to ask Mr Stevens to continue to work through his notice period, or for me to ask him not to work out his notice period,” Marks said.

“I felt it was important, given what had happened, that I asked him not to work out his period, and to pay him his contractual entitlement to do so.

“I felt it was important that we move forward with new leadership. So I didn’t want to continue Mr Stevens in that role.”

Stevens, whose total remuneration for the financial year was $864,394, was replaced by Reuters executive Simon Robinson last month after a 19-year career at the public broadcaster. His base salary was $529,202, according to the annual report.

Marks told senators “mistakes” were made in the production of programs by former Four Corners reporter Mahmood Fazal but the entire leadership of Four Corners had now been replaced.

The ABC has removed several programs made by the sacked bikie turned journalist because of concerns over his use of anonymous interviewees.

“We did a review of Mr Fazal’s work and found substantial flaws in much of that work,” he said.

“I think we can take confidence that there are many great people who do work for Four Corners. And with new editorial leadership, we are obviously very confident as to its future.”

The ABC said it was reviewing its editorial guidance about the use of anonymous sources in light of the Fazal incident.

Sally Neighbour, a former Four Corners executive producer, alleged in the Monthly that “an associate of Fazal played different roles in different stories, disguised behind a mask”.

Fazal has previously said he stands by his reporting. In July, he said he was “shocked” by the removal of the two Four Corners episodes and that he believed the ABC’s process and decisions “set a worrying precedent for the organisation’s independence and commitment to public-interest journalism”.

australia.title: Albanese concedes $6m golf club grant in his electorate was not to contain ‘raw sewage’
australia.snippet: Grant part of $560m invitation-only scheme transparency advocates say largely funded projects in Labor-held seats Follow our Australian p...
australia.content:
Anthony Albanese has admitted he got it wrong after telling parliament a $6m grant to a golf club in his electorate was to stop “raw sewage” going into the nearby river.

The grant given to Marrickville golf club in Sydney’s inner-west is under scrutiny as part of a larger $560m invitation-only grants scheme, which transparency advocates say largely funded projects promised at the 2025 election in Labor-held seats.

Infrastructure department officials told a Senate estimates hearing on Monday afternoon the $6m grant given to the club in Albanese’s electorate did not fund works to prevent raw sewage from flowing into the nearby river, contrary to the prime minister’s claims.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

“I can confirm that sewerage is not a component of this grant,” the department’s assistant secretary, Jacinta McDonald, said.

The assistant regional development minister, Anthony Chisholm, defended the prime minister’s response, saying the scope had changed since the local council’s original proposal.

“I think that was part of the original plan. But as often happens, as the scope of these sorts of announcements happen, the scope can change, and the New South Wales government, is my understanding, stepped in in support of the sewerage work,” Chisholm said.

First reported by the ABC, Albanese, who holds honorary social membership at the club, has swatted away any criticism that he influenced, or benefitted from, the decision, which was signed off by another minister.

In question time in early September, the prime minister told the house the money would go toward “an environmental project stopping raw sewage going into the Cooks River during flooding”.

“[The golf club] has existed for a long time, almost a 100 years, and they have a septic tank because it is on the floodplain, when it floods in Marrickville raw sewage flows into the Cooks River – that is what the funding is for,” Albanese said in another response to questions about his involvement in the decision-making process.

The prime minister was grilled repeatedly by the opposition about the grant in question time on Tuesday afternoon and the shadow energy minister, Dan Tehan, accused the prime minister of misleading the parliament, and urged him to correct the record.

In response, Albanese conceded “it was not correct” to say the funding was for sewerage works but said it was a matter for the infrastructure department, and noted the council was finalising the design of the project – including improvements to the clubhouse, stormwater harvesting, a new toilet and landscaping.

The NSW government committed in September 2025 to address sewerage infrastructure at the club, he said.

“I’m advised that the club, of course, has a long history. And indeed, in the media release announcing the project, it spoke about the venue’s last major remodel being in 1947. So this is a local club, owned by the council,” Albanese said.

“The [federal] funding was going to be for sewerage. The New South Wales government have stepped in, which is appropriate given that New South Wales run water and sewerage.”

australia.title: Asthma deaths reach decade-high levels and number of Australians dying of dementia grows
australia.snippet: Dementia, including Alzheimer’s disease, accounted for more than 10% of all deaths for the first time, new data reveals Get our breaking ...
australia.content:
Dementia has accounted for more than 10% of all deaths for the first time, while the number of people dying from asthma is at decade-high levels, new data published by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) reveals.

There were 188,421 deaths registered in 2025. Of these, 19,019 deaths were caused by dementia, including Alzheimer’s disease, the ABS deaths data released on Tuesday shows. It has been the leading cause of death in Australia since 2024.

The other leading causes of death in 2025 were ischaemic heart diseases, cerebrovascular diseases (such as stroke), lung cancer and chronic respiratory diseases.

Dementia Australia’s chief executive, Prof Tanya Buchanan, said there was an urgent need to act on dementia, given it was a leading public health issue.

“The data underlines the critical need for more recognition and funding to support people living with dementia, their families and carers,” Buchanan said.

There are an estimated 446,500 Australians currently living with dementia, and a further 1.7 million people involved in their care, she said.

“Despite the growing impact of dementia, investment in specific services, supports and prevention have not kept the same pace, and the stigma that surrounds dementia continues,” she said.

“This needs to change.”

The data also revealed the highest number of asthma deaths recorded in a decade.

There were 484 Australians who died from asthma in 2025, up from 478 deaths in 2024.

Women account for almost two-thirds of asthma deaths, and almost two-thirds of all dementia deaths.

Asthma Australia’s CEO, Kate Miranda, said poorly controlled asthma increases the risk and is a preventable reason behind many asthma-related deaths.

“We have effective treatments and clear clinical guidelines, yet too many Australians are not getting the care they need to stay well,” she said.

Research has found the proportion of adults with well-controlled asthma has been falling, with many using little or no preventer treatment. Adherence among those using inhaled corticosteroids was also worsening, Miranda said.

Too many people only used asthma-reliever medications, and rely on it for their symptoms.

“But it doesn’t treat the underlying inflammation,” Miranda said.

“People, especially those with mild cases, think ‘it’s just asthma’, so they don’t get regular checkups and talk to their GP about their medication. People might take preventer medication on high pollen days or when they have a cold, but then they don’t take it otherwise.”

She said people should be aware that asthma guidelines have shifted to recommend anti-inflammatory reliever (Air) therapy, an anti-inflammatory that also treats symptoms.

“People, especially older Australians, are still using medications they had as a child without being aware guidelines have changed and better options exist,” Miranda said.

Drug-induced deaths also remained a public health issue in 2025, rising to 2,063 deaths from 2,007 deaths in 2024.

The ABS’s head of mortality statistics, Lauren Moran, said while opioids and benzodiazepines continue to be the most common drug classes involved in these deaths, there has been substantial growth in people dying after using stimulants, including methamphetamine.

Suicide remained the leading cause of premature death for both males and females in 2025, with men accounting for almost three-quarters of these deaths.

  • In Australia, support is available at Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, Lifeline on 13 11 14, and at MensLine on 1300 789 978

australia.title: Bridget McKenzie fears MPs will ‘retreat from the public square’ following alleged attack on Helen Haines – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Political debate should be ‘robust but respectful’, ...
australia.content:
Opposition continues pressure over golf club grant

The manager of opposition business in the house, Dan Tehan returns and asks the prime minister to “stop the spin and admit he was wrong”.

It’s met with much grumblings from the government benches and the speaker, Milton Dick, asks Tehan to refer to a point, saying he does not want to set a precedent where “you can just do a statement, and then that’s a question”. Anthony Albanese answers:

After we made the commitment to the club which included fixing this issue - which has been an issue since 1947 - the state government have stepped in. That is a good thing.

Key events

  • 7h ago

    What we learned today, Tuesday 27 October

  • 7h ago

    Bridget McKenzie says she fears MPs will ‘retreat from the public square’ following alleged attack on Haines

  • 7h ago

    Anne Aly says politicians interacting with public 'cornerstone of our Australian democracy'

  • 9h ago

    Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time

    Labor’s Peter Khalil ejected after interrupting Angus Taylor’s question

    Speaker urges MPs to ‘remember why we’re here’ and not to fall back into ‘bad habits’
